claim: At physiological temperature, endocytosis kinetics at hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals show a bi-phasic dependence on electrical activity.
source: Here we show that at physiological temperature endocytosis kinetics at hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals show a bi-phasic dependence on electrical activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Endocytosis accelerates for the first 15–25 APs during bursts of action potential firing.
source: Endocytosis accelerates for the first 15–25 APs during bursts of action potential firing, after which it slows with increasing burst length creating an optimum stimulus for this kinetic parameter.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2D showing acceleration phase at physiological temperature.

claim: After 15-25 APs, endocytosis slows with increasing burst length creating an optimum stimulus for this kinetic parameter.
source: Endocytosis accelerates for the first 15–25 APs during bursts of action potential firing, after which it slows with increasing burst length creating an optimum stimulus for this kinetic parameter.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2 showing slowing phase with larger stimuli.

claim: Activity-dependent acceleration of endocytosis is only prominent at physiological temperature.
source: We show that activity-dependent acceleration is only prominent at physiological temperature and that the mechanism of this modulation is based on the dephosphorylation of dynamin 1.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data at 30°C vs 37°C shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The mechanism of activity-dependent acceleration is based on the dephosphorylation of dynamin 1.
source: We show that activity-dependent acceleration is only prominent at physiological temperature and that the mechanism of this modulation is based on the dephosphorylation of dynamin 1.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with phosphomimetic and phospho-deficient dynamin 1 mutants shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nerve terminals in which dynamin 1 and 3 have been replaced with dynamin 1 harboring dephospho-mimetic mutations (S774/778A) eliminate the acceleration phase by setting endocytosis at an accelerated state.
source: Nerve terminals in which dynamin 1 and 3 have been replaced with dynamin 1 harboring dephospho- or phospho-mimetic mutations in the proline-rich domain eliminate the acceleration phase by either setting endocytosis at an accelerated state or a decelerated state, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing phospho-deficient mutant behavior.

claim: Nerve terminals in which dynamin 1 and 3 have been replaced with dynamin 1 harboring phospho-mimetic mutations (S774/778D) eliminate the acceleration phase by setting endocytosis at a decelerated state.
source: Nerve terminals in which dynamin 1 and 3 have been replaced with dynamin 1 harboring dephospho- or phospho-mimetic mutations in the proline-rich domain eliminate the acceleration phase by either setting endocytosis at an accelerated state or a decelerated state, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing phosphomimetic mutant behavior.

claim: At small CNS nerve terminals, the size of the recycling SV pool is often limited.
source: At small CNS nerve terminals the size of the recycling SV pool is often limited (Harata et al., 2001; de Lange et al., 2003; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2004; Kim and Ryan, 2010; Denker et al., 2011) and therefore control of steps in SV recycling will likely prove important in setting overall synaptic performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Control of steps in SV recycling will likely prove important in setting overall synaptic performance.
source: At small CNS nerve terminals the size of the recycling SV pool is often limited (Harata et al., 2001; de Lange et al., 2003; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2004; Kim and Ryan, 2010; Denker et al., 2011) and therefore control of steps in SV recycling will likely prove important in setting overall synaptic performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limited pool size and cited literature.

claim: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals, synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in a dynamin-dependent fashion.
source: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in a dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011), clathrin (Granseth et al., 2006) and AP-2 dependent fashion (Kim and Ryan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals, synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in a clathrin-dependent fashion.
source: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in a dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011), clathrin (Granseth et al., 2006) and AP-2 dependent fashion (Kim and Ryan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals, synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in an AP-2 dependent fashion.
source: At hippocampal and cortical nerve terminals synaptic vesicles are retrieved largely in a dynamin (Ferguson et al., 2007; Raimondi et al., 2011), clathrin (Granseth et al., 2006) and AP-2 dependent fashion (Kim and Ryan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Endocytosis occurs in a probabilistic fashion.
source: Single vesicle retrieval studies (Balaji and Ryan, 2007) demonstrated that endocytosis occurs in a probabilistic fashion, and the mean endocytosis time constant for large bursts (100 AP 10 Hz) is a cell-wide property that can vary significantly from neuron to neuron (Armbruster and Ryan, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior single vesicle retrieval studies.

claim: The mean endocytosis time constant for large bursts (100 AP 10 Hz) is a cell-wide property that can vary significantly from neuron to neuron.
source: Single vesicle retrieval studies (Balaji and Ryan, 2007) demonstrated that endocytosis occurs in a probabilistic fashion, and the mean endocytosis time constant for large bursts (100 AP 10 Hz) is a cell-wide property that can vary significantly from neuron to neuron (Armbruster and Ryan, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Numerous studies have revealed a modulatory role for Ca2+ in endocytosis at nerve terminals in different synaptic preparations.
source: Numerous studies have revealed a modulatory role for Ca2+ in endocytosis at nerve terminals in different synaptic preparations (Balaji et al., 2008; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Wu et al., 2009; Yamashita et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2009) although the precise steps at which Ca2+ acts in this process have not been identified.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The precise steps at which Ca2+ acts in endocytosis have not been identified.
source: Numerous studies have revealed a modulatory role for Ca2+ in endocytosis at nerve terminals in different synaptic preparations (Balaji et al., 2008; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Wu et al., 2009; Yamashita et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2009) although the precise steps at which Ca2+ acts in this process have not been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field based on literature review.

claim: The direction of Ca2+ modulation on endocytosis is in dispute.
source: The direction of the Ca2+ modulation is also in dispute, some studies suggest an accelerating role of Ca2+, (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001; Wu et al., 2009) while others suggest that Ca2+ slows endocytosis (Balaji et al., 2008; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Sun et al., 2002; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting prior studies.

claim: Some studies suggest an accelerating role of Ca2+ on endocytosis.
source: The direction of the Ca2+ modulation is also in dispute, some studies suggest an accelerating role of Ca2+, (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001; Wu et al., 2009) while others suggest that Ca2+ slows endocytosis (Balaji et al., 2008; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Sun et al., 2002; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some studies suggest that Ca2+ slows endocytosis.
source: The direction of the Ca2+ modulation is also in dispute, some studies suggest an accelerating role of Ca2+, (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001; Wu et al., 2009) while others suggest that Ca2+ slows endocytosis (Balaji et al., 2008; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Sun et al., 2002; Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A number of proteins with Ca2+ sensing domains have been implicated in SV endocytosis, including synaptotagmin, calmodulin, and calcineurin.
source: Although a number of proteins with Ca2+ sensing domains have been implicated in SV endocytosis (synaptotagmin, calmodulin, calcineurin) direct links connecting endocytic behavior to consequences of Ca2+ sensing have not been established.
evidence: This is a statement about proteins implicated in the process based on prior knowledge.

claim: Direct links connecting endocytic behavior to consequences of Ca2+ sensing have not been established.
source: Although a number of proteins with Ca2+ sensing domains have been implicated in SV endocytosis (synaptotagmin, calmodulin, calcineurin) direct links connecting endocytic behavior to consequences of Ca2+ sensing have not been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Endocytosis has a pronounced acceleration phase with increasing number of action potentials used to elicit exocytosis.
source: We took advantage of the ability to map endocytosis kinetics with high fidelity using a pHluorin-tagged synaptic vesicle protein to show that endocytosis has a pronounced acceleration phase with increasing number of action potentials used to elicit exocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The initial acceleration phase of endocytosis is followed by a gradual slowing with increasing stimulus number.
source: This initial acceleration phase is followed by a gradual slowing with increasing stimulus number.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Previous studies had missed the acceleration phase, in part due to the variability of endocytosis time constants across different neurons.
source: Our previous studies had missed this acceleration phase, in part due to the variability of endocytosis time constants across different neurons and in part owing to the fact that it is only readily apparent at physiological temperatures (37°C).
evidence: This is a reflection on prior work and explanation for why the acceleration phase was not previously observed.

claim: The acceleration phase is only readily apparent at physiological temperatures (37°C).
source: Our previous studies had missed this acceleration phase, in part due to the variability of endocytosis time constants across different neurons and in part owing to the fact that it is only readily apparent at physiological temperatures (37°C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data at different temperatures shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both phases of stimulus-dependent endocytosis are modulated by Ca2+.
source: We show that both phases of stimulus-dependent endocytosis are modulated by Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by experiments varying external Ca2+ and using EGTA shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The existence of two phases with opposite sign implies endocytosis has an optimal minimal value that is tuned by calcium-dependent processes.
source: The existence of two phases with opposite sign implies endocytosis has an optimal minimal value that is tuned by calcium-dependent processes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed bi-phasic behavior.

claim: Dynamin was identified in a search for proteins whose phosphorylation decreases upon Ca2+ entry at nerve terminals.
source: Dynamin, a mechano-chemical enzyme that plays a key role in membrane fission (Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012), was identified in a search for proteins whose phosphorylation decreases upon Ca2+ entry at nerve terminals (Robinson and Dunkley, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Dynamin is a mechano-chemical enzyme that plays a key role in membrane fission.
source: Dynamin, a mechano-chemical enzyme that plays a key role in membrane fission (Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012), was identified in a search for proteins whose phosphorylation decreases upon Ca2+ entry at nerve terminals (Robinson and Dunkley, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior review.

claim: Two specific serines in dynamin's proline rich domain (S774 and S778) are substrates for the calcium-dependent phosphatase calcineurin and the proline-directed serine/threonine kinase CDK5.
source: Subsequent studies demonstrated two specific serines in dynamin's proline rich domain as substrates for the calcium-dependent phosphatase calcineurin and the proline-directed serine/threonine kinase CDK5 (Graham et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Eliminating the two major brain dynamin isoforms (dynamin 1 and 3) results in a dramatic (>10-fold) slowing in endocytosis kinetics.
source: This strong phenotype allowed us to sensitively probe the ability of different dynamin isoforms to restore endocytic function in response to varying stimulus conditions. We show that mutating the two key phosphorylated serines in dynamin 1 to either alanine or aspartate both rescue the major endocytic defect of the dynamin 1/3 KO however they both eliminate the activity-dependent acceleration of endocytosis kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study and data in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutating the two key phosphorylated serines in dynamin 1 to either alanine or aspartate both rescue the major endocytic defect of the dynamin 1/3 KO.
source: We show that mutating the two key phosphorylated serines in dynamin 1 to either alanine or aspartate both rescue the major endocytic defect of the dynamin 1/3 KO however they both eliminate the activity-dependent acceleration of endocytosis kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Mutating the two key phosphorylated serines in dynamin 1 to either alanine or aspartate both eliminate the activity-dependent acceleration of endocytosis kinetics.
source: We show that mutating the two key phosphorylated serines in dynamin 1 to either alanine or aspartate both rescue the major endocytic defect of the dynamin 1/3 KO however they both eliminate the activity-dependent acceleration of endocytosis kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Dynamin 1 is a critical substrate in activity-dependent modulation of synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
source: These studies thus pinpoint dynamin 1 as a critical substrate in activity-dependent modulation of synaptic vesicle endocytosis and that it forms a basis for fine-tuning the retrieval process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with phosphorylation mutants.

claim: Dynamin 1 forms a basis for fine-tuning the synaptic vesicle retrieval process.
source: These studies thus pinpoint dynamin 1 as a critical substrate in activity-dependent modulation of synaptic vesicle endocytosis and that it forms a basis for fine-tuning the retrieval process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: vG-pH fluorescence is quenched by the acidic lumen of the synaptic vesicle (pH 5.6).
source: vG-pH fluorescence is quenched by the acidic lumen of the synaptic vesicle (pH 5.6).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pHluorin reporter.

claim: Upon exocytosis, vG-pH vesicular fluorescence increases ∼20-fold.
source: Upon exocytosis the vesicular fluorescence increases ∼20-fold and is requenched by reacidification after endocytosis (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study establishing the reporter properties.

claim: vG-pH fluorescence is requenched by reacidification after endocytosis.
source: Upon exocytosis the vesicular fluorescence increases ∼20-fold and is requenched by reacidification after endocytosis (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The endocytic time constant can be deconvolved from reacidification and measured from the fluorescence decay after stimulation.
source: The endocytic time constant can be deconvolved from reacidification and measured from the fluorescence decay after stimulation (Granseth et al., 2006; Balaji et al., 2008) where it has been shown in numerous studies to follow simple single exponential decay kinetics over a broad range of stimulus conditions (Balaji and Ryan, 2007; Armbruster and Ryan, 2011; Yao et al., 2011; Kwon and Chapman, 2012; Willox and Royle, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior methodological studies.

claim: Endocytosis has been shown in numerous studies to follow simple single exponential decay kinetics over a broad range of stimulus conditions.
source: The endocytic time constant can be deconvolved from reacidification and measured from the fluorescence decay after stimulation (Granseth et al., 2006; Balaji et al., 2008) where it has been shown in numerous studies to follow simple single exponential decay kinetics over a broad range of stimulus conditions (Balaji and Ryan, 2007; Armbruster and Ryan, 2011; Yao et al., 2011; Kwon and Chapman, 2012; Willox and Royle, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Changes in reacidification rates are only expected to minimally impact endocytosis time constant estimates.
source: Changes in reacidification rates are only expected to minimally impact endocytosis time constant estimates (see 'Materials and methods') and for the relevant stimulus conditions asynchronous release would unlikely affect the measures of endocytosis (Atluri and Ryan, 2006; Granseth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by analysis in Materials and methods section.

claim: For the relevant stimulus conditions, asynchronous release would unlikely affect the measures of endocytosis.
source: Changes in reacidification rates are only expected to minimally impact endocytosis time constant estimates (see 'Materials and methods') and for the relevant stimulus conditions asynchronous release would unlikely affect the measures of endocytosis (Atluri and Ryan, 2006; Granseth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The exponential endocytic decay was slower for 100 AP stimulation compared to 10 AP stimulation at 10 Hz at 30°C.
source: Comparison of fluorescence recovery profiles for exocytosis triggered with a 100 AP and 10 AP at 10 Hz (at 30°C) at the same boutons however revealed that the exponential endocytic decay was slower for the larger stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The endocytic time constant shows a continuous trend of gradual slowing with increasing stimulus number from 10 to 100 AP.
source: Experiments carried out at an individual set of boutons for a range of stimuli (10, 25, 50, and 100 AP) showed that this trend was continuous, with gradual slowing of the endocytic time constant (τendo) with increasing stimulus number (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The degree of slowing of endocytosis was most easily parameterized as a linear dependence on the number of action potentials used to drive exocytosis.
source: The degree of slowing was most easily parameterized as a linear dependence on the number of action potentials used to drive exocytosis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by linear fits shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both the degree of slowing (slope in s/AP) and the extrapolated fastest time constant expected at 1 AP (intercept) vary significantly across neurons.
source: We examined this dependence on stimulus number across collections of boutons from many individual neurons (N = 44) and found both the degree of slowing (i.e., the slope in s/AP) and the extrapolated fastest time constant expected at 1 AP (the intercept) to vary significantly across neurons (Figure 1C) but were uncorrelated with each other.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C across 44 cells.

claim: The degree of slowing (slope) and the extrapolated fastest time constant at 1 AP (intercept) are uncorrelated with each other across neurons.
source: We examined this dependence on stimulus number across collections of boutons from many individual neurons (N = 44) and found both the degree of slowing (i.e., the slope in s/AP) and the extrapolated fastest time constant expected at 1 AP (the intercept) to vary significantly across neurons (Figure 1C) but were uncorrelated with each other.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean degree of slowing for the population of neurons was 0.058 ± 0.004 s/AP.
source: The mean degree of slowing for the population of neurons was 0.058 ± 0.004 s/AP.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of data from 44 neurons.

claim: The activity-dependent slowing of endocytosis is enhanced under conditions that would lead to more elevated intracellular calcium.
source: Comparisons of the slowing behavior in the same synapses for stimuli delivered in 4 mM compared to 2 mM external Ca2+ demonstrated that this inhibition of endocytosis appears to be enhanced under conditions that would lead to more elevated intracellular calcium (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data comparing 2 mM and 4 mM Ca2+ shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The activity-dependent slowing was always steeper when stimuli were delivered in 4 mM compared to 2 mM external Ca2+.
source: These experiments revealed that the activity-dependent slowing was always steeper when stimuli were delivered in the higher Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: On average, the slope of activity-dependent slowing increased by ∼700% when external Ca2+ was increased from 2 mM to 4 mM.
source: On average (n = 9) the slope increased by ∼700% (Figure 1E) while the intercept was unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E across 9 cells.

claim: The intercept of the linear relationship between τendo and stimulus number was unchanged when external Ca2+ was increased from 2 mM to 4 mM.
source: On average (n = 9) the slope increased by ∼700% (Figure 1E) while the intercept was unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Buffering intracellular Ca2+ with EGTA-AM slowed endocytosis compared to control across stimuli.
source: These experiments revealed that buffering intracellular Ca2+ slowed endocytosis compared to control across stimuli but eliminated slowing as a function of stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Buffering intracellular Ca2+ with EGTA-AM eliminated slowing of endocytosis as a function of stimulation.
source: These experiments revealed that buffering intracellular Ca2+ slowed endocytosis compared to control across stimuli but eliminated slowing as a function of stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Incubation with EGTA-AM unmasked a modest acceleration phase for the lowest stimuli (25 AP).
source: Additionally incubation with EGTA-AM unmasked a modest acceleration phase for the lowest stimuli (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The observed single AP τendo was slower than that obtained at 25 AP.
source: The observed single AP τendo was slower than for that obtained at 25 AP (Figure 2A), as well as than that predicted from the linear regression at higher stimulus levels (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The observed single AP τendo was slower than that predicted from the linear regression at higher stimulus levels.
source: The observed single AP τendo was slower than for that obtained at 25 AP (Figure 2A), as well as than that predicted from the linear regression at higher stimulus levels (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: There are two distinct phases of activity-dependence: an acceleration of endocytosis for stimuli >1 AP and a slowing for stimuli > approximately 10 AP.
source: Taken together these data thus demonstrate two distinct phases of activity-dependence: an acceleration of endocytosis for stimuli >1 AP and a slowing for stimuli > approximately 10 AP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: At physiological temperature (37°C), endocytosis accelerated by 42 ± 7% (N = 9) going from 5 AP to 25 AP.
source: At physiological temperature, on average, endocytosis accelerated by 42 ± 7% (N = 9) going from 5 AP to 25 AP and then slowed by 18 ± 4% (N = 8) at the 100 AP stimulus level.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of data at 37°C.

claim: At physiological temperature (37°C), endocytosis slowed by 18 ± 4% (N = 8) at the 100 AP stimulus level compared to 25 AP.
source: At physiological temperature, on average, endocytosis accelerated by 42 ± 7% (N = 9) going from 5 AP to 25 AP and then slowed by 18 ± 4% (N = 8) at the 100 AP stimulus level.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of data at 37°C.

claim: At 37°C, the prominent slowing phase of endocytosis present at 30°C required larger stimuli (300 AP) to show obvious (55 ± 20% [N = 7]) slowing when compared to 100 AP 10 Hz.
source: The prominent slowing phase of endocytosis present at 30°C however was still observed at 37°C but it required larger stimuli (300 AP) to show obvious (55 ± 20% [N = 7]) slowing when compared to 100 AP 10 Hz.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing different temperatures and stimulus levels.

claim: Increasing external Ca2+ from 2 mM to 4 mM accelerated the post-stimulus endocytosis kinetics significantly for single AP stimulation at 37°C.
source: We tested this notion explicitly by comparing the endocytic time constant for single AP stimulation at 2 mM and 4 mM Ca2+ at 37°C. These experiments showed that increasing Ca2+ accelerated the post-stimulus endocytosis kinetics significantly (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The acceleration of endocytosis persists for at least 15 s after a 5 AP burst.
source: These experiments revealed that the acceleration of endocytosis caused by 5 AP persists for at least 15 s, but is lost for intervals >30 s.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The acceleration of endocytosis caused by a 5 AP burst is lost for inter-burst intervals >30 s.
source: These experiments revealed that the acceleration of endocytosis caused by 5 AP persists for at least 15 s, but is lost for intervals >30 s.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The impact of a single 5 AP burst on accelerating endocytosis persisted for at least 20 s.
source: The impact of a single 5 AP burst on accelerating endocytosis however persisted for at least 20 s, as τendo for a second 5 AP burst was accelerated to the same extent as providing a continuous 10 AP burst even if the second burst was delivered 20 s later.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: For a 30 s inter-burst interval, measurements showed no significant acceleration of endocytosis.
source: Measurements for a 30 s inter-burst interval however showed no significant acceleration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The acceleration of endocytosis persists for ∼20 s between stimuli but is dissipated after ∼30 s.
source: These experiments show that the acceleration persists for ∼20 s between stimuli but is dissipated after ∼30 s.
evidence: This is a summary of data from Figure 3.

claim: Elevations in intracellular Ca2+ following a 5 AP burst decay on much faster time scales (<1 s).
source: Given that elevations in intracellular Ca2+ following a 5 AP burst decays on much faster time scales (<1 s) these data imply that Ca2+ is likely acting through a second messenger system to control endocytosis in the acceleration phase.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about calcium dynamics.

claim: Ca2+ is likely acting through a second messenger system to control endocytosis in the acceleration phase.
source: Given that elevations in intracellular Ca2+ following a 5 AP burst decays on much faster time scales (<1 s) these data imply that Ca2+ is likely acting through a second messenger system to control endocytosis in the acceleration phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence time of acceleration compared to calcium dynamics.

claim: Dynamin 1 is constitutively phosphorylated at serines 774 and 778 by Cdk5.
source: Dynamin 1, the founding member of the dephosphin family and by far the most abundant neuronal dynamin, is constitutively phosphorylated at serines 774 and 778 by Cdk5 and dephosphorylated in a stimulus- induced manner at the same sites by the Ca2+ dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Dynamin 1 is dephosphorylated in a stimulus-induced manner at serines 774 and 778 by the Ca2+ dependent phosphatase calcineurin.
source: Dynamin 1, the founding member of the dephosphin family and by far the most abundant neuronal dynamin, is constitutively phosphorylated at serines 774 and 778 by Cdk5 and dephosphorylated in a stimulus- induced manner at the same sites by the Ca2+ dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Liu et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: A major effect of dynamin 1 phospho-regulation is to control the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin.
source: A major effect of this phospho-regulation is to control the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin, whose binding to dephospho-dynamin is abolished by phosphorylation (Anggono et al., 2006; Anggono and Robinson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Syndapin binding to dephospho-dynamin is abolished by phosphorylation.
source: A major effect of this phospho-regulation is to control the interaction of dynamin 1 with syndapin, whose binding to dephospho-dynamin is abolished by phosphorylation (Anggono et al., 2006; Anggono and Robinson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dephosphorylation of dynamin after a stimulatory burst has been shown to persist for ∼40 s under certain stimulus conditions.
source: Interestingly, dephosphorylation of dynamin after a stimulatory burst has been shown to persist for ∼40 s under certain stimulus conditions (Robinson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Dynamin 1/3 DKO mice have severely impaired endocytosis.
source: We previously showed that dynamin 1/3 DKO mice have severely impaired endocytosis; however, nerve terminals lacking these major dynamin isoforms are still able to undergo multiple rounds of vesicle recycling (Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study and data in Figure 4A.

claim: Nerve terminals lacking dynamin 1 and 3 are still able to undergo multiple rounds of vesicle recycling.
source: We previously showed that dynamin 1/3 DKO mice have severely impaired endocytosis; however, nerve terminals lacking these major dynamin isoforms are still able to undergo multiple rounds of vesicle recycling (Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The absence of both dynamin 1 and 3 results in a severe impairment of endocytosis, which can be fully rescued by re-introduction of dynamin 1.
source: We re-examined endocytosis in dynamin 1/3 DKO neurons at 37°C which showed a very similar phenotype to our previous studies (Figure 4A): the absence of both dynamin 1 and 3 results in a severe impairment of endocytosis, which can be fully rescued by re-introduction of dynamin 1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mouse cortical neurons show very similar endocytosis behavior as rat hippocampal neurons with the exception that the slowing phase was much less pronounced and was only evident at much higher stimulus levels.
source: These experiments showed very similar behavior as rat hippocampal neurons with the exception that the slowing phase was much less pronounced and was only evident at much higher stimulus levels (see below).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutations of serines 774 and 778 to alanine and aspartate mimic the dephosphorylated and phosphorylated states respectively with respect to dynamin 1's ability to bind syndapin.
source: Previous studies have shown that mutations of these serines to alanine and aspartate mimic the dephosphorylated and phosphorylated states respectively with respect to dynamin 1's ability to bind syndapin (Anggono et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Both phosphomimetic (S774/778D) and phospho-deficient (S774/778A) mutants could efficiently rescue the severe dynamin 1/3 DKO endocytosis defect.
source: Although both phosphomimetic (S774/778D) and phospho-deficient (S774/778A) mutants could efficiently rescue the severe dynamin 1/3 DKO endocytosis defect, neither showed any activity dependent acceleration (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Neither phosphomimetic (S774/778D) nor phospho-deficient (S774/778A) mutants showed any activity dependent acceleration.
source: Although both phosphomimetic (S774/778D) and phospho-deficient (S774/778A) mutants could efficiently rescue the severe dynamin 1/3 DKO endocytosis defect, neither showed any activity dependent acceleration (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The phosphomimetic form of dynamin 1 was effectively locked in a slower endocytic state.
source: The phosphomimetic form was effectively locked in a slower endocytic state, while the phospho-deficient form was faster across all stimuli (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,E.

claim: The phospho-deficient form of dynamin 1 was faster across all stimuli.
source: The phosphomimetic form was effectively locked in a slower endocytic state, while the phospho-deficient form was faster across all stimuli (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,E.

claim: Neurons expressing mutants of dynamin 1 that lock the phosphorylation sites in a specific state do not undergo stimulus-dependent regulation.
source: Thus, neurons expressing mutants of dynamin 1 that lock the phosphorylation sites in a specific state do not undergo stimulus-dependent regulation and constitutively proceed at overall faster (phospho-deficient mutant) or slower (phospho-mimetic mutant) endocytic speeds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from data in Figure 4.

claim: Neurons expressing phospho-deficient dynamin 1 mutant constitutively proceed at overall faster endocytic speeds.
source: Thus, neurons expressing mutants of dynamin 1 that lock the phosphorylation sites in a specific state do not undergo stimulus-dependent regulation and constitutively proceed at overall faster (phospho-deficient mutant) or slower (phospho-mimetic mutant) endocytic speeds.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,E.

claim: Neurons expressing phosphomimetic dynamin 1 mutant constitutively proceed at overall slower endocytic speeds.
source: Thus, neurons expressing mutants of dynamin 1 that lock the phosphorylation sites in a specific state do not undergo stimulus-dependent regulation and constitutively proceed at overall faster (phospho-deficient mutant) or slower (phospho-mimetic mutant) endocytic speeds.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,E.

claim: Dynamin 2 was only able to partially rescue the 100 AP 10 Hz time constant in dynamin 1/3 DKO neurons.
source: Dynamin 2, which has different activity dependent phosphorylation sites (Chircop et al., 2011), was only able to partially rescue the 100 AP 10 Hz time constant and was not tested further.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dynamin 2 has different activity dependent phosphorylation sites than dynamin 1.
source: Dynamin 2, which has different activity dependent phosphorylation sites (Chircop et al., 2011), was only able to partially rescue the 100 AP 10 Hz time constant and was not tested further.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Increasing the stimulus number from 100 AP to 300 AP showed a slowing of endocytosis for all conditions (control, dynamin 1 rescue, phosphomimetic, and phospho-deficient).
source: Increasing the stimulus number from 100 AP to 300 AP showed a slowing of endocytosis for all conditions similar to the relationship described at 30°C (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No difference was detected in the size of the recycling pool of synaptic vesicles between control, dynamin 1, phosphomimetic, or phospho-deficient rescue.
source: Using the bafilomycin method (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001) we detected no difference in the size of the recycling pool of synaptic vesicles or in the rate of exocytosis between control, dynamin 1, phosphomimetic, or phospho-deficient rescue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference was detected in the rate of exocytosis between control, dynamin 1, phosphomimetic, or phospho-deficient rescue.
source: Using the bafilomycin method (Sankaranarayanan and Ryan, 2001) we detected no difference in the size of the recycling pool of synaptic vesicles or in the rate of exocytosis between control, dynamin 1, phosphomimetic, or phospho-deficient rescue (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dynamin 1 phosphorylation sites that were previously demonstrated to be calcineurin substrates are critical specifically for the acceleration phase during brief action potential bursts.
source: Our experiments show that dynamin 1 phosphorylation sites that were previously demonstrated to be calcineurin substrates are critical specifically for the acceleration phase during brief action potential bursts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation mutant experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 accelerates the kinetics of endocytosis without fundamentally changing the endocytic properties.
source: The dephosphorylation accelerates the kinetics of endocytosis without fundamentally changing the endocytic properties suggesting that this represents a tuning of the mechanism rather than a distinct pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that both mutants rescue the major defect but differ in kinetics.

claim: Dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 represents a tuning of the endocytic mechanism rather than a distinct pathway.
source: The dephosphorylation accelerates the kinetics of endocytosis without fundamentally changing the endocytic properties suggesting that this represents a tuning of the mechanism rather than a distinct pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The dynamin 1/3 DKO provides the ideal background to test the significance of the phosphorylation sites.
source: The dynamin 1/3 DKO provides the ideal background to test the significance of the phosphorylation sites, as it is necessary to also remove dynamin 3 since it has a similar phospho-box motif as dynamin 1 (Larsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citation.

claim: It is necessary to remove dynamin 3 in addition to dynamin 1 since dynamin 3 has a similar phospho-box motif as dynamin 1.
source: The dynamin 1/3 DKO provides the ideal background to test the significance of the phosphorylation sites, as it is necessary to also remove dynamin 3 since it has a similar phospho-box motif as dynamin 1 (Larsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Analysis in dynamin 1/3 DKO nerve terminals indicates that bulk endocytosis proceeds unimpaired in the absence of dynamin.
source: Although recent studies implicate dynamin's phosphorylation in controlling bulk endocytosis, analysis in dynamin 1/3 DKO nerve terminals indicates that this form of endocytosis proceeds unimpaired in the absence of dynamin (Yumei Wu, Shawn Ferguson and Pietro De Camilli, in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by citation to unpublished work.

claim: Endocytosis is stochastic and the mean time for endocytosis is determined by a single rate-limiting step.
source: Analysis of single synaptic vesicle retrieval demonstrated that endocytosis is stochastic and the mean time for endocytosis is determined by a single rate-limiting step (Balaji and Ryan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Dynamin is considered to be a critical enzyme in endocytic membrane fission.
source: As dynamin is considered to be a critical enzyme in endocytic membrane fission (Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012), the fact that endocytosis kinetics can be accelerated by dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 suggests that under these conditions membrane fission, or another dynamin-dependent event, is the rate limiting step in endocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior review.

claim: Under conditions where dynamin 1 dephosphorylation accelerates endocytosis, membrane fission or another dynamin-dependent event is the rate limiting step in endocytosis.
source: As dynamin is considered to be a critical enzyme in endocytic membrane fission (Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012), the fact that endocytosis kinetics can be accelerated by dephosphorylation of dynamin 1 suggests that under these conditions membrane fission, or another dynamin-dependent event, is the rate limiting step in endocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of dynamin and the observed acceleration.

claim: Phosphorylation of dynamin at serines 774 and 778 abolishes the interaction with the F-BAR protein syndapin.
source: Phosphorylation of dynamin at serines 774 and 778 abolishes the interaction with the F-BAR protein syndapin and dephosphorylation promotes it (Anggono et al., 2006; Anggono and Robinson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dephosphorylation of dynamin at serines 774 and 778 promotes the interaction with the F-BAR protein syndapin.
source: Phosphorylation of dynamin at serines 774 and 778 abolishes the interaction with the F-BAR protein syndapin and dephosphorylation promotes it (Anggono et al., 2006; Anggono and Robinson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The cooperative participation of syndapin and dephosphorylated dynamin improves the efficiency of the endocytic process.
source: Our data therefore suggest that the cooperative participation of syndapin and dephosphorylated dynamin improves the efficiency of the endocytic process: when dynamin cannot bind syndapin (phosphomimetic mutation) no acceleration occurs, while when dynamin can interact with syndapin even at rest (phospho-deficient mutation), endocytosis is already fast and no stimulus-dependent acceleration occurs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with phosphorylation mutants.

claim: When dynamin cannot bind syndapin (phosphomimetic mutation), no acceleration of endocytosis occurs.
source: Our data therefore suggest that the cooperative participation of syndapin and dephosphorylated dynamin improves the efficiency of the endocytic process: when dynamin cannot bind syndapin (phosphomimetic mutation) no acceleration occurs, while when dynamin can interact with syndapin even at rest (phospho-deficient mutation), endocytosis is already fast and no stimulus-dependent acceleration occurs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing no acceleration for phosphomimetic mutant.

claim: When dynamin can interact with syndapin even at rest (phospho-deficient mutation), endocytosis is already fast and no stimulus-dependent acceleration occurs.
source: Our data therefore suggest that the cooperative participation of syndapin and dephosphorylated dynamin improves the efficiency of the endocytic process: when dynamin cannot bind syndapin (phosphomimetic mutation) no acceleration occurs, while when dynamin can interact with syndapin even at rest (phospho-deficient mutation), endocytosis is already fast and no stimulus-dependent acceleration occurs.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing fast endocytosis without acceleration for phospho-deficient mutant.

claim: Genetic ablation of syndapin 1, the major syndapin isoform expressed in brain, revealed a number of pleotropic phenotypes consistent with a failure to properly recruit dynamin to membranes.
source: Consistent with this scenario however, genetic ablation of syndapin 1, the major syndapin isoform expressed in brain, revealed a number of pleotropic phenotypes consistent with a failure to properly recruit dynamin to membranes (Koch et al., 2011) and syndapin is one of the proteins whose levels are more strongly reduced in mice that lack dynamin 1 and 3 (Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Syndapin is one of the proteins whose levels are more strongly reduced in mice that lack dynamin 1 and 3.
source: Consistent with this scenario however, genetic ablation of syndapin 1, the major syndapin isoform expressed in brain, revealed a number of pleotropic phenotypes consistent with a failure to properly recruit dynamin to membranes (Koch et al., 2011) and syndapin is one of the proteins whose levels are more strongly reduced in mice that lack dynamin 1 and 3 (Raimondi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The Ca2+ dependent slowing phase of endocytosis was more prominent at lower temperatures.
source: The Ca2+ dependent slowing phase we observed was more prominent at lower temperatures and agrees well with previous findings that show Ca2+ inhibition of endocytosis (Balaji et al., 2008; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data at different temperatures and citations to prior studies.

claim: The Ca2+ dependent slowing phase agrees well with previous findings that show Ca2+ inhibition of endocytosis.
source: The Ca2+ dependent slowing phase we observed was more prominent at lower temperatures and agrees well with previous findings that show Ca2+ inhibition of endocytosis (Balaji et al., 2008; von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994; Sun et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The Ca2+ sensor for the slowing mechanism is not known.
source: The Ca2+ sensor for this mechanism is not known, although we showed that it is not affected by setting dynamin's phosphorylation state at the calcineurin sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The Ca2+ dependent slowing mechanism is not affected by setting dynamin's phosphorylation state at the calcineurin sites.
source: The Ca2+ sensor for this mechanism is not known, although we showed that it is not affected by setting dynamin's phosphorylation state at the calcineurin sites.
evidence: This is supported by data showing slowing at 300 AP for all conditions in Figure 4F.

claim: Manipulation of calcineurin and CDK5 enzymatic activities impacted synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
source: Previously a number of studies examined the role of the specific enzymes, calcineurin and CDK5, that control dynamin phosphorylation (Liu et al., 1994; Tan et al., 2003; Tomizawa et al., 2003), in controlling vesicle recycling. Although manipulation of these enzymatic activities impacted synaptic vesicle endocytosis, it is seems likely that these manipulations do not solely alter dynamin activity given that they target numerous substrates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Manipulations of calcineurin and CDK5 do not solely alter dynamin activity given that they target numerous substrates.
source: Previously a number of studies examined the role of the specific enzymes, calcineurin and CDK5, that control dynamin phosphorylation (Liu et al., 1994; Tan et al., 2003; Tomizawa et al., 2003), in controlling vesicle recycling. Although manipulation of these enzymatic activities impacted synaptic vesicle endocytosis, it is seems likely that these manipulations do not solely alter dynamin activity given that they target numerous substrates.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known substrate promiscuity of these enzymes.

claim: Both calcineurin and CDK5 profoundly modulate Ca2+ influx.
source: Recent studies have recently shown for example that both these enzymes profoundly modulate Ca2+ influx (Kim and Ryan, 2013) precluding simple interpretations of such pharmacological manipulations on endocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: At 37°C, synaptic vesicle retrieval appears to be optimized for brief action potential bursts.
source: Our data indicate that at 37°C synaptic vesicle retrieval appears to be optimized for brief action potential bursts and that the basis for this tuning is based on a balance of calcineurin activation vs an additional calcium-dependent inhibitory effect that dominates during prolonged stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bi-phasic behavior observed at physiological temperature.

claim: The basis for optimization of synaptic vesicle retrieval for brief bursts is based on a balance of calcineurin activation vs an additional calcium-dependent inhibitory effect that dominates during prolonged stimulation.
source: Our data indicate that at 37°C synaptic vesicle retrieval appears to be optimized for brief action potential bursts and that the basis for this tuning is based on a balance of calcineurin activation vs an additional calcium-dependent inhibitory effect that dominates during prolonged stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing acceleration and slowing phases.

claim: Dynamin appears to be centrally important in short term optimization of endocytosis.
source: Furthermore dynamin appears to be centrally important in this short term optimization as preventing changes in the phosphorylation at two key serines in dynamin 1 eliminates this tuning of endocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation mutant experiments.

claim: Preventing changes in the phosphorylation at two key serines in dynamin 1 eliminates the tuning of endocytosis.
source: Furthermore dynamin appears to be centrally important in this short term optimization as preventing changes in the phosphorylation at two key serines in dynamin 1 eliminates this tuning of endocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C,D showing elimination of acceleration in phosphorylation mutants.

claim: Cells might tune their endocytic profile to be optimized for individual firing patterns.
source: This data compels one to speculate that cells might tune their endocytic profile to be optimized for individual firing patterns.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed optimization.

claim: Tuning of endocytic profile could be achieved by altering the balance of CDK5 and calcineurin activity.
source: The tuning could be achieved by altering the balance of CDK5 and calcineurin activity as has been demonstrated for certain forms of homeostatic plasticity (Kim and Ryan, 2010), or by altering routes of Ca2+ entry or clearance.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior study on homeostatic plasticity.

claim: Tuning of endocytic profile could be achieved by altering routes of Ca2+ entry or clearance.
source: The tuning could be achieved by altering the balance of CDK5 and calcineurin activity as has been demonstrated for certain forms of homeostatic plasticity (Kim and Ryan, 2010), or by altering routes of Ca2+ entry or clearance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the role of calcium in the observed effects.

claim: The phosphorylation sites in dynamin (serines 774 and 778) are well conserved across species with a nervous system.
source: These phosphorylation sites in dynamin are well conserved across species with a nervous system suggesting that that endocytic optimization is a fundamental property of nervous system function.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation.

claim: Conservation of dynamin phosphorylation sites suggests that endocytic optimization is a fundamental property of nervous system function.
source: These phosphorylation sites in dynamin are well conserved across species with a nervous system suggesting that that endocytic optimization is a fundamental property of nervous system function.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary conservation.

claim: A change in reacidification from 1.6 s to 2.6 s introduces a +8% error in the measurement of endocytosis for a 10 s time constant.
source: To assess the contribution of changing reacdification times to our endocytosis fits, we ran simulations based upon the biexponential model of synaptic vesicle endocytosis (Granseth et al., 2006) and our fitting protocols. A change in reacdification from 1.6 s to 2.6 s introduces a +8% error in the measurement of endocytosis for a 10 s time constant, suggesting that it is unlikely to explain our observations.
evidence: This is based on simulations using a biexponential model.

claim: Changes in reacidification are unlikely to explain the observed acceleration and slowing of endocytosis.
source: A change in reacdification from 1.6 s to 2.6 s introduces a +8% error in the measurement of endocytosis for a 10 s time constant, suggesting that it is unlikely to explain our observations.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation results.
